I'll settle on Wound as the safer parent for "trauma incision" since any incision is fundamentally a wound, regardless of whether the traumatic connection holds. Moving to the SSTI (skin/soft tissue infection) row, I'm weighing whether trauma-associated infections should link to infected wound or just the infection process, since not all such infections are strictly wound infections.

Row 5: trauma-related necrotizing fasciitis is more a disease entity than a wound per se—NF arises from infection of soft tissue rather than being the wound itself, so I lean toward none here, though that creates tension with how I treated row 3's SSTI, which also technically covers NF cases. I need to decide whether to keep these judgments consistent or treat each term on its specific framing.

Since trauma-related SSTI is essentially infection following traumatic wounds in the literature, I'll keep rows 3 and 7 as wound infection, but row 5 (NF) stays none since it's an infection of fascia rather than the wound site itself.

Row 6 is trauma-related infection, classified as material entity, so it stands. Row 8, trauma-related wound, parallels traumatic wound so it stands too. Row 9, traumatic amputation, counts as material entity since the stump injury is a wound. For row 10, traumatic brain injury, I'm reconsidering — TBI includes things like concussion and diffuse axonal injury that aren't wounds in the wound-care sense, and since injury isn't offered as a category here, I'll mark this as none.

Row 11, traumatic cavity-type defect, is clearly a traumatic wound from trauma, so it stands. Row 12, traumatic closed degloving injury (Morel-Lavallée), keeps skin intact and counts as a closed wound, so it stands as well. Row 13, traumatic dental injury, is trickier — it's mostly hard tissue fractures and luxation rather than a wound in the typical wound-care sense, though it could still count as tissue disruption under the broader definition.

Since Wound sits under Injury and the two are distinguished, not every injury qualifies as a wound, so I'll mark both row 10 and row 13 as none. Rows 14 through 16 (traumatic extremity skin defect, traumatic foot wound, traumatic hypertrophic scar) all map cleanly to wound or scar siblings, so those stand. Row 17, traumatic injury, runs into the same broader-than-wound issue since it can include fractures and TBI, so the wound classification doesn't quite fit.

Row 18, traumatic laceration, stays since lacerations are inherently traumatic and fall under traumatic wound. Row 19 is trickier — traumatic lesion could mean anything from a wound to a bone bruise or nerve lesion, so for consistency with row 17 I'm leaning toward marking it none as well, though I'm second-guessing whether that's too strict.

Row 20, traumatic oral ulcer, is an oral mucosal ulcer caused by trauma, so it counts as a traumatic wound and stands.

I'm settling on treating the healing response as the same concept as wound healing. The healing scale and score entries seem fine as information content entities tied to assessment and classification processes, so those stand. For stimulation, I'll note it's likely none since it's not every instance a treatment. Time post-grafting is just a duration datum, so none there. Tool fits as a material entity for treatment, and the promoting effect works as a therapeutic function, so both stand.

For "wound healing/closure," closure is a surgical treatment process while healing is the biological one—since the term bridges both, I'll lean toward treating it as the same as wound healing rather than is_a, for consistency with the similar "wound healing/repair" entry which is essentially wound healing itself.

For wound hematoma, it's straightforwardly a hematoma occurring in a wound, so is_a Hematoma fits. Wound hydration level is just a moisture measure, distinct from maceration (edge softening), so I don't think either relation applies there.

Moving to "vascular deficit" as a quality, I'm comparing it against ischemia and degree of tissue perfusion. A vascular deficit might refer to arterial insufficiency leading to reduced blood supply, so I'm considering whether it's effectively synonymous with ischemic quality or something more structural.

Since vascular deficit could also encompass venous insufficiency rather than purely ischemia, I decide the parent mapping is too risky and go with none. For vascular density increase, I'm noting it could stem from angiogenesis, vasculogenesis, or capillary recruitment, not just one process.

Not every vascular disorder reduces perfusion—venous insufficiency is treated separately from angiopathy here, so vascular disorder is broader. I'll change it to pathological disorder instead.

Row 5: Vascular endothelial cell stays under cell, that's fine.

Row 6: VEGF-driven angiogenesis is_a angiogenesis stands, no wound-healing context required here.

Row 7: for vascular endothelial tubulogenesis, I'm weighing whether this is in vitro tube formation (Matrigel assay) versus in vivo blood vessel morphogenesis—GO has endothelial tube morphogenesis under generic tube morphogenesis, and since these abstracts likely describe in vitro assays, the safer parent is probably tube morphogenesis rather than blood vessel morphogenesis.

Row 8: vascular etiology as a "role" doesn't fit—aetiopathogenetic role applies to molecular entities, while vascular etiology describes the cause classification of a wound, not a role of an entity, so this gets none.

Row 9: flow-mediated dilation is_a vasodilation stands, since even though FMD is a measurement test, it's typed as an endothelium-dependent process involving smooth muscle relaxation.

Row 10 is about vascular formation and whether it maps to blood vessel morphogenesis as the formation of anatomical structures.

Rows 11-13: vascular function doesn't match physiological role since function and role are distinct BFO categories—vascular function is a vessel's function, not a molecular entity role. Vascular grafting is a surgical procedure, not a circulatory physiological process, so none applies there either. Vascular granulation relates to granulation tissue formation in well-vascularized tissue.

Row 14: vascular groin surgery fits under surgical treatment for vascular disease, so disease treatment process stands. Row 15: vascular growth maps to vasculature development as an increase in vessel size. Row 16: vascular healing dynamic is ambiguous—it could mean endothelial repair after stenting rather than angiogenesis-driven wound healing, so I'm leaning toward none for this one.

Row 17: vascular homeostasis fits as a circulatory process, so that stands. Row 18: vascular human cell is just a cell type, stands. Row 19: vascular impairment is tricky—it's proposed as material disease entity but feels more like a reduced function state than a true disease, so I'm inclined to say none here too.

Row 20: vascular inflammation is_a inflammatory response, not strictly wound-healing related, so this stays with 6.

For the stenting procedure, I note that it's about maintaining blood vessel diameter rather than an actual biological process, so no fitting category applies. The surgery row holds as a surgical treatment process. For venous symptom, I'm considering whether deviation from normal captures something like leg heaviness or pain.

For wound formation, I'm weighing whether it matches the wound development process that has venous insufficiency as part of its causation.

The distinction is subtle but I'll let the classification stand since wound formation could reasonably be seen as part of the disease course. For row 20, venous wound treatment classified as a wound treatment process stands fine.

Wound length is a straightforward measure of extent, so that stands. Wound lesion seems essentially synonymous with wound, so I'd mark that as same. Wound level is trickier—it could mean anatomic location or depth/tissue involvement, so I'm still weighing that one.

Going through the margin-related entries, wound margin aligns with wound edge, so it stands. Margin advance is more about epithelial migration during re-epithelialization rather than contraction, and there's no clean parent category offered, so I'm leaning toward none. Margin tissue reasonably maps to wound edge as a material entity, so that stands too.

For wound mat, I'm uncertain whether it refers to a dressing or something else, but accepting it as stands seems reasonable. Wound matrix likely points to a dermal matrix product, which is a distinct material entity worth considering separately.

Wound maturation seems to fit better as part of the wound-healing-related physiological process category rather than standing alone, so I want to change that classification. Wound microbial burden also seems to align with the quality/degree category already used elsewhere, so I'm updating its classification to match.

Moving through the remaining rows, wound microbiota dynamic doesn't fit colonization clearly, microenvironment reprogramming seems more like a therapeutic intervention than tissue remodeling, wound modality is ambiguous between treatment and imaging contexts, and wound modulation is too vague to classify confidently — I'm leaving these without a clear assignment for now and moving on to evaluate wound monitoring next.

Wound monitoring fits reasonably under diagnostic process since it involves repeated assessment. Wound morphology stands as a quality attribute. Wound myiasis management should be classified as a treatment process rather than strictly mechanical debridement, since it could involve occlusion or medication too. For wound necrosis, I'm weighing whether it's better captured as necrotic material versus necrotic wound bed, since necrosis can affect wound edges as well as the bed itself.

Wound necrosis is necrotic material found within a wound, so I'll change its classification to that. For wound necrosis type, it's really a categorization like dry versus wet necrosis, so it's more of an information entity than a grade or stage — after weighing classification result and disease stage options, I'll leave it unclassified since type isn't really a grading concept.

Rows 18 through 20 look fine as stated.

I'm also weighing whether "wound type" could be the output of a classification process—a recorded classification result—since surgical wound classes (like CDC clean/contaminated categories) function similarly to grades in this ontology's structure, even though strictly speaking type differs from stage.

Row 11, volume decrease isn't necessarily wound contraction since granulation filling can also reduce volume without the centripetal edge movement that defines contraction, so neither process label quite fits and I'll leave it unmapped. Row 12, wound volume reduction looks more like a measured outcome than a treatment itself, since it's typically reported as a percentage change rather than the intervention producing it.

Row 13, wound wall convergence is trickier since in NPWT literature it's often described as a mechanically-induced macrodeformation effect rather than the physiological contraction process driven by myofibroblasts, even though the terminology overlaps heavily with classic wound contraction language.

Row 14, wound width is a one-dimensional extent, so that classification stands. Row 15, wound's actual size falls under the size classification, which also stands.

Row 16 brings up the wound's opposing tissue surface — the facing surfaces of the wound walls — and I'm weighing whether these count as wound edges or something distinct, like opposing surfaces in an incision.

For rows 17-20, WIfI classification and its method work as types of wound classification scales, so those stand, and WIfI clinical stage, derived from a combination of factors, still counts as a wound classification grade category.

Moving to the ischemic diabetic foot ulcer case, I'm weighing whether it should fall under diabetic foot ulcer or ischemic wound, since it presumably qualifies as both.

For the treatment-resistant wound case, chronic wound still fits well—a wound that failed to heal despite treatment matches the definition of failing to progress through healing phases in orderly fashion.

Looking at "treatments material entity," this term seems odd, possibly an artifact referring to materials used in wound treatment; I'm uncertain whether it's wound-specific enough to justify its current parent.

Now I'm considering a treatment process combining standard of care with something else, likely still fitting under wound treatment processes.

For Treg/Th17 balance, this makes sense as a ratio of immune cell populations inhering in tissue as a relative proportion.

Trephination—drilling into bone or nail to relieve pressure or promote healing—fits under excision as physical removal of substance, consistent with wound care applications like exposed bone management.

For trial dressing, it fits as a wound dressing used in clinical trials. As for trial drug, I'm weighing whether it counts as an investigational drug versus a clinical drug product bearing a therapeutic role—leaning toward treating it as a drug product intended for therapeutic use rather than strictly the "clinical drug" category.

Next I'm considering the Triangle of Wound Assessment, a framework covering wound bed, edge, and periwound skin—it's more of an assessment tool than a formal classification scale.

Row 20: Triboelectric wearable device stands as a device.
